name: Ancient Rome
title: Social Hierarchy of Ancient Rome: From Emperor to Enslaved

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You command the legions, appoint the governors and answer to no court, but your power rests on the army’s loyalty, and several of your predecessors were murdered.
tiers.kid: The emperor commanded the army, made the laws and had his face on the coins.
tiers.rise: In law any man the Senate and the army accepted could rule. In practice emperors came from the senatorial order, and in the 3rd century more and more often from the army, as soldiers raised their own commanders to the throne.
tiers.why: The emperor was in name the “first citizen” (princeps) and in fact the master of the state.

tiers.name: Senators
tiers.you: You own estates worth more than a million sesterces, wear the broad purple stripe and may govern a province or command a legion, if the emperor trusts you.
tiers.kid: Senators were rich landowners who advised the emperor and governed the provinces.
tiers.rise: A rich equestrian entered when the emperor granted him the broad stripe or enrolled him among the former magistrates. A senator who fell below the property qualification, or offended the emperor, lost his seat.

tiers.name: Equestrians
tiers.you: Your fortune passes 400,000 sesterces; you wear a gold ring and may serve the emperor as an officer, a tax official or even prefect of Egypt.
tiers.kid: Equestrians, or knights, were wealthy men who ran the emperor’s offices, money and some of his armies.
tiers.rise: Sons of town councillors, veteran chief centurions and rich provincials entered the order by the emperor’s grant. The most successful equestrians, or their sons, could be raised to the Senate.
tiers.why: The equestrians, or knights, formed the second order.

tiers.name: Town councillors
tiers.you: You sit on your town’s council, help gather its taxes, and are expected to pay for its baths, games or temples from your own purse.
tiers.kid: Every Roman town had a council of rich local men who ran its markets, temples and festivals.
tiers.rise: Wealthy local men entered the council, often after holding a local magistracy. Freedmen were generally barred, but their sons could enter.
tiers.why: Every Roman town had a council of decurions, drawn from the leading local families and bound by a property qualification that each town set for itself.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You have signed on for twenty-five years in an auxiliary unit, with regular pay, a bounty at the end, and Roman citizenship for you and your children when you are discharged.
tiers.kid: Roman soldiers served for about 25 years and were given land or money when they retired.
tiers.rise: Enlisting gave a poor citizen a steady wage and a provincial a path to citizenship. A capable soldier could become a centurion and, as chief centurion, an equestrian.
tiers.why: The army was a professional force of long-serving volunteers.

tiers.name: Free people
tiers.you: You farm a few acres or work at a trade, pay your taxes and look to a patron for help; if you are convicted of a crime, the law can flog you or send you to the mines.
tiers.kid: Most Romans were farmers, craftspeople and shopkeepers who worked hard to feed their families.
tiers.rise: Wealth from trade, a soldier’s career or a patron’s favour could lift a family onto a town council within a generation or two. Debt and bad harvests pushed free farmers into tenancy.
tiers.why: Most of the empire’s free people were small farmers, tenants, labourers, craftsmen and shopkeepers.

tiers.name: Freed slaves
tiers.you: You were born a slave and won your freedom, and with it Roman citizenship, but you still owe duties to your former owner and may never hold office; your children will be free of that mark.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people who were set free became Roman citizens, and their children were born free.
tiers.rise: The children of freedmen were freeborn citizens and could enter the town councils, and their grandsons sometimes reached equestrian rank.
tiers.why: A slave freed by a Roman citizen became a citizen, something Greek observers found remarkable, but not an equal one.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to another person, who can sell you, punish you and keep your children; if your work and your owner allow, you may save enough to buy your freedom.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; some were later set free.
tiers.rise: Freedom came only by manumission: as a reward, by purchase with the slave’s own savings, or in the owner’s will. It made the freed slave a Roman citizen.
